newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica maize harvest seen dragging into September.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica maize harvest seen dragging into September.

text.p: South Africa's 1997 maize harvest has been delayed by up to three weeks due to heavy rain in parts of the producing area, industry officials said on Monday.

A normal crop would see harvesting being completed at the end of July but the National Maize Producers' Organisation (Nampo) said in some parts of the country harvesting could continue into August and even early September.
"The crop has been delayed by about three to four weeks," Nampo general manager Giel van Zyl said.
He said in the eastern and north west areas of South Africa, farmers were struggling to start harvesting because maize had been saturated by heavy rains.
But in the main maize-producing areas of Gauteng province and the Free State the harvest was in full swing.
"The weather we are experiencing at the moment means that the harvest will be delayed and harvesting will take place during July and August, maybe even into September," van Zyl said.
Independent forecaster Weather Services Corp on Monday predicted a few isolated showers in the south and said that recent drier conditions would favour the remaining harvest in South Africa.
Maize future prices were unaffected by the lateness of the crop, South African Futures Exchange (Safex) Rob Blondin said.
"The market hasn't really shown that. But today the July price for yellow has stayed still. It has come down a little bit, 5.00 rand a tonne for yellow maize."
July yellow maize on Safex remained steady to trade at 553.00 rand. July white was bid at 590 rand and offered at 600 from a 590 settlement on Friday.
"We haven't seen any major price trends on our market," Blondin added.
Maize millers said the lateness of the crop had not affected operations.

"We have had some carryover so we are not affected by the lateness of the crop. I understand the other larger millers are in a similar position," said Schalk Pienaar, procurement head at Premier Milling, one of South Africa's biggest milling firms.
"But those who haven't (got carryover stocks) are getting in a tighter and tighter position in terms of stock holding and price."
He said the delay in the harvest had upped spot prices, which were experiencing further upward pressure from early export commitments by farming co-operatives.
Central co-operative Unie Graan said in May co-operatives had already committed 70 percent of this year's surplus to the export market.
Shipping sources estimate that South Africa will export around 1.2 million tonnes of maize this season (May-April) out of an estimated commercial crop of 7.660 million tonnes.
But this will depend on the level of damage caused by recent snowfalls and unseasonal rains.
Already some 250,000 tonnes of mostly white maize has been exported to Kenya and Venezuela since the start of the new season on May 1.
But shipping sources said the bulk of the maize sent was left over from last year's bumper crop, due to the harvest delay.
South Africa's official crop estimate committee last month left its crop estimate unchanged at 7.660 million tonnes.
